title: Presenting your design
idea: Presenting a design means walking listeners from the problem to your classes and trade-offs, so they can follow, question and trust every choice you made.
points: Open with the problem and the use cases, not with the classes.
Show the class diagram, then trace one request through it.
Name each trade-off you made and the option you rejected.
End with how the design grows, such as recurring bookings.

items.label: Problem
items.text: Employees need a room for a time slot, with no double booking.

items.label: Use cases
items.text: Search free rooms, book, cancel, notify attendees. Say what is out of scope.

items.label: Classes
items.text: Show the class diagram: `BookingService` in the middle, repositories and `ConflictPolicy` beside it.

items.label: One flow
items.text: Trace `book(...)`: policy check, `save`, then each `BookingListener` hears `onBooked`.

items.label: Trade-offs
items.text: Why `ConflictPolicy` is a strategy; why errors are unchecked with a stable `code()`.

items.label: Next steps
items.text: Which class would change for recurring bookings, and which stay untouched; then take questions.

pitfalls: Do not read code line by line; trace one request through the diagram instead.
Answer a challenge with the requirement it serves, not with a pattern name.
Rehearse once with a timer so the trade-offs are not cut for time.
takeaway: Problem, use cases, classes, one flow, trade-offs, next steps.

starters: How do I answer "why not just use inheritance here" during my talk?
What should I do if a reviewer finds a bug while I present?
How much code should I show in a design presentation?
